newsitem.title: NEPAL: Nepal politicians huddle in bid to form government.
newsitem.headline: Nepal politicians huddle in bid to form government.

text.p: Major political parties in Nepal plunged into meetings on Friday after the centre-left government was voted out and King Birendra set a deadline of March 10 for the formation of a new government.
Madhav Kumar Nepal, General Secrtary of the opposition Unified Marxist-Leninist (UML) party said the communists were taking stock of the situation before making a decision.
"We have time. We are not in a hurry," Nepal told Reuters.
Earlier on Friday Nepal's King Birendra set a deadline of March 10 for the country's political parties to stake a claim to power after the centrist government lost a confidence vote.

"His Majesty the King has called upon members of the House of Representatives to make a submission to His Majesty by 6 p.m. (1215 GMT) on March 10, clearly establishing one's ability to command support and confidence from a majority of members of the House of Represenatives," the Royal Palace said in a communique.

The king issued the communique, which was broadcast on state-owned Radio Nepal, after prime minister Sher Bahadur Deuba resigned on Thursday following the defeat of his 17-month-old coalition in a confidence vote.
King Birendra asked the three-party coalition headed by Deuba's centrist Nepali Congress party to continue in power until the formation of a new council of ministers.
No single party controls a majority in Nepal's parliament which emerged from general elections in November 1994.
Nepali Congress officials said the central working committee, the chief executive organ of the party, would meet later on Friday to discuss the political scenario.
The communist UML party, which ruled for 10 months until Deuba's coalition took office in September 1995, was expected to try to stake a claim to reassume power.

Deuba's government received 101 votes against a required minimum of 103 during voting in the 205-seat lower house on the motion, which he had moved to try to demonstrate the coalition's majority. A total of 92 deputies voted against.
The Nepali Congress party, which has 87 seats, lost its majority last December following a split in the ranks of one of its two partners, the Rashtriya Prajatantra Party (RPP), which had 19 seats.
Surya Bahadur Thapa, President of the RPP, said the position of the various political parties, each struggling with internal differences, was not clear.
"Nothing has emerged yet," Thapa said adding that by late on Friday or Saturday a clearer picture should start emerging.

The UML and its allies control 94 votes in the parliament elected in November 1994, when the Himalayan kingdom held its second general elections after ushering in democracy in 1990. The UML then formed a minority government.

But it was defeated in September 1995, when Deuba assumed power by cobbling together a three-party coalition with crucial support from the RPP, which was once close to the monarchy. Nepal now has British-style constitutional monarchy.

Rajeswor Devakota, who belongs to an RPP faction oppposed to Deuba, said on Thursday that there was a possibility of a coalition between the RPP and UML. The faction has five of RPP's 19 members, and did not take part in Thursday's voting.
UML's high-level standing committee met soon after Thursday's vote to try and form a new government.
"All options are open," UML general secretary Madhav Kumar Nepal told Reuters. "The possibility of a new coalition with any major party will be discussed (by the party)," he said.
